2025.clinched: Race 2, Hockenheimring, 2025, the last race of the season
2025.note: Güven took the title by four points in the closest finish the revived series has produced, 192 to Lucas Auer’s 188 with Maro Engel a further four back on 184. He won three races across the eight rounds, at Zandvoort, the Sachsenring and finally Hockenheim, where the last win of the year was also the one that settled it. He drove a Porsche for Manthey EMA.

2024.season: eight rounds and sixteen races in 2024, and a first title for a Lamborghini
2024.note: Bortolotti won five races to finish on 238 points, ahead of Kelvin van der Linde on 221 and Maro Engel on 203, driving for SSR Performance. He was the first Italian champion since Nicola Larini in 1993.

2023.note: Preining settled it at the last round, where he won both races, and finished the year on 246 points to Bortolotti’s 213 and Ricardo Feller’s 179. He drove a Porsche for Manthey EMA, and Porsche took the manufacturers’ championship as well. It was the first season with the ADAC as promoter.

2022.season: eight rounds and sixteen races in 2022, the year team orders were banned
2022.note: Van der Linde won four races, both at the Lausitzring plus the Nürburgring and Hockenheim openers, to finish on 164 points ahead of Lucas Auer on 153 and René Rast on 149, driving a BMW M4 GT3 for Schubert Motorsport. The rules had changed over the winter in direct response to the previous season’s finale: team orders were banned outright.

2021.clinched: Norisring, 10 October 2021, at the final round, and disputed afterwards
2021.note: Götz won the title by three points, 230 to Liam Lawson’s 227, with Kelvin van der Linde third on 208, in a finale that produced a first-corner collision between his two rivals and team orders from Mercedes-AMG in the closing laps. The controversy was enough that team orders were banned outright for the following season. It was the first year the DTM ran to Group GT3 rules, after the two-year Class 1 experiment proved so expensive that both Audi and BMW withdrew manufacturer support; Ferrari, McLaren and Lamborghini came in as privateers instead.

2020.season: a third title in 2020, and seven race wins
2020.note: Rast won seven races for Audi Sport Team Rosberg to take a third championship in four years, matching Bernd Schneider’s record of four titles in the revived series only in the sense of joining the very short list above two. It was the last season under Class 1 regulations.

2019.season: a second title in 2019, and seven race wins
2019.note: Rast won seven races for Audi Sport Team Rosberg, a year after losing the championship by four points despite taking six consecutive victories, a series record. He had won the title as a rookie in 2017, which makes this the middle of three championships in four seasons.

2018.clinched: Hockenheimring, 2018, at the final round, with a third place
2018.note: Paffett took the title by four points, 255 to René Rast’s 251, with Paul di Resta third on 233 across twenty races. Rast had mounted the most spectacular losing run the series has seen, six consecutive wins and a new record, and still fell short. It was Mercedes-Benz’s final DTM season before the marque left for Formula E, and Paffett’s second championship, thirteen years after his first.

2017.season: a first title in 2017, in a first full season
2017.note: Rast won three races for Audi Sport Team Rosberg and the championship in his debut year in the series, which is where a run of three titles in four seasons began.

2016.note: Wittmann reclaimed the title at the last round, finishing fourth while his rival Edoardo Mortara won the race, which was not enough. He took three wins in the BMW M4 DTM for BMW Team RMG, and it was his second championship in three years.

2015.season: eighteen races across nine events in 2015, opening and closing at Hockenheim
2015.note: Wehrlein won two races and finished on 169 points, 19 clear of Jamie Green on 150 with Mattias Ekström third on 147, driving for HWA. The season ran from 2 May to 18 October at the same circuit.

2014.clinched: the third-to-last event of 2014, with a sixth place
2014.note: Wittmann settled his first championship with three events still to run, which is unusually early for this series, and finished 50 points clear of Mattias Ekström. He won four races in the BMW M4 DTM for BMW Team RMG.

2013.clinched: Circuit Park Zandvoort, 29 September 2013, at the penultimate round
2013.note: Rockenfeller won his only championship with two race wins, at Brands Hatch and Moscow, finishing on 142 points to Augusto Farfus’s 116 and Bruno Spengler’s 82 across ten rounds. The season introduced a drag reduction system to the series and took it to Russia for the first time.

2012.clinched: Hockenheimring, 21 October 2012, by winning the final race
2012.note: Spengler won the title by four points, 149 to Gary Paffett’s 145, with Jamie Green third on 121, and did it by winning the last race of the year. He took five wins in all, at the Lausitzring, the Nürburgring, Oschersleben, Valencia and Hockenheim. BMW had returned to the championship that season for the first time since 1994, an eighteen-year absence, and won it at the first attempt.

2011.clinched: Hockenheimring, 23 October 2011, at the final round
2011.note: Tomczyk won four races, at the Red Bull Ring, the Lausitzring, Brands Hatch and Hockenheim, and finished on 72 points to Mattias Ekström’s 52 and Bruno Spengler’s 51. The detail that makes it remarkable is the car: he ran a 2008-specification Audi A4 for Team Phoenix while the factory drivers had the newer machinery.

2010.clinched: Shanghai, 28 November 2010, at the final round
2010.note: Di Resta took the title by four points, 71 to Gary Paffett’s 67, with Bruno Spengler third on 66. He had trailed Spengler by fifteen points after four races, led by the ninth round, and at the finale finished second while Paffett won and Spengler, having crashed in qualifying, could only manage thirteenth. He won four races, and announced a move to Formula One shortly afterwards.

2009.season: ten rounds in 2009, and a successful defence
2009.note: Scheider won two races for Abt Sportsline and beat Gary Paffett to the title by five points, becoming only the second driver after Bernd Schneider to defend a DTM championship.

2008.season: a first title in 2008, by four points
2008.note: Scheider won three races in the Audi A4 DTM for Abt Sportsline and beat Paul di Resta to the championship by four points.

2007.season: a second title in 2007, and three race wins
2007.note: Ekström won three races in the Audi A4 DTM for Abt Sportsline to take his second championship, three years after the first.

2006.season: a fifth title in 2006, from only two race wins
2006.note: Schneider won just two races and still took the championship, which was his fifth in all and his fourth since the series was revived in 2000, driving the AMG-Mercedes C-Klasse for HWA. No other driver has won this championship as often.

2005.season: eleven races in 2005, and a first title
2005.note: Paffett won six races and finished on 84 points, 13 clear of Mattias Ekström with Tom Kristensen third on 56. Cars built to the older 2000-2003 specification were banned that year, Mika Häkkinen arrived in the series for his first season, and Opel announced it was leaving shortly after the year ended.

2004.season: a first title in 2004, and the first for Audi since the series was revived
2004.note: Ekström won four races in the Audi A4 DTM for Abt Sportsline, beating the Mercedes pair of Gary Paffett and Christijan Albers. The first four championships of the revived series had all gone to Mercedes drivers; this was the first that did not.

2003.season: a fourth title in 2003, from two race wins
2003.note: Schneider won two races in the AMG-Mercedes CLK for HWA and took the championship for the third time in four seasons of the revived series.

2002.clinched: Hockenheimring, 6 October 2002, at the final round
2002.note: Aïello won the title by six points, 70 to Bernd Schneider’s 64, with Mattias Ekström third on 50, after taking six main-race wins. The format that year gave each of the ten weekends a 30-kilometre qualifying race and a 100-kilometre main race. He drove for Abt Sportsline, a privateer Audi entry, and beat the factory Mercedes operation at HWA, which took the teams’ championship instead.

2001.season: a second title in 2001, and three race wins
2001.note: Schneider won three races in the AMG-Mercedes CLK-DTM for HWA and made it two championships from the first two seasons of the revived series.

2000.season: the first season of the revived series, in 2000, and six race wins
2000.note: Schneider won six races in the AMG-Mercedes CLK-DTM for HWA to take the first championship after the DTM returned, four years after the old series had collapsed. He had also won the last DTM title before the break, in 1995.

1996.season: the 1996 season, run as the International Touring Car Championship, and the last before the series folded
1996.note: With the FIA’s blessing the DTM had become a world championship, racing from Hockenheim to São Paulo, and Reuter won it in an Opel Calibra on 218 points, thirteen clear of Bernd Schneider’s Mercedes and 38 ahead of Alessandro Nannini’s Alfa Romeo. Opel took the makes’ title too and called it the biggest success in its racing history. Class 1 rules required a purpose-built 2.5-litre V6 and elaborate electronics with almost nothing in common with a road car, which earned the cars the nickname Formula One with a roof and made them unaffordable. Two days before the Mugello race in late September, Opel joined Alfa Romeo in announcing its withdrawal, and that was the end of the series until 2000.

1995.season: a first title in 1995, and the last before the series collapsed
1995.note: Schneider won five races for the D2 Privat-Team AMG Mercedes to take the last DTM championship of the original era. He would win the first of the revived era as well, five years later.

1994.season: a third title in 1994, in the first year of the Mercedes C-Class
1994.note: Ludwig won the championship in the Mercedes C-Class V6 for AMG Mercedes D2 Privat Team, his third DTM title after 1988 and 1992 and his second in three years. He was known in Germany as König Ludwig.

1993.season: ten rounds and twenty races in 1993, and eleven wins
1993.note: Larini won eleven races, a series record, and finished on 261 points to Roland Asch’s 204 and Bernd Schneider’s 172, in the debut season of the Alfa Romeo 155 V6 TI. It was also the first year under FIA Class 1 rules, which capped engines at six cylinders and 2.5 litres. Alfa Romeo took the manufacturers’ championship.

1992.season: a second title in 1992, in the Mercedes 190E Evo 2
1992.note: Ludwig took the championship in the Mercedes 190E 2.5-16 Evolution II for AMG, four years after his first title with Ford and two before his third.

1991.season: twelve rounds and twenty-four races in 1991, won in an Audi
1991.note: Biela finished on 174 points to Klaus Ludwig’s 166 and Hans-Joachim Stuck’s 158, winning at the Alemannenring, twice at Hockenheim and at Donington Park in the Audi V8 quattro. Mercedes-Benz took the manufacturers’ championship, so the two titles went different ways, and it was the second consecutive drivers’ title for the V8 quattro.

1990.season: twelve rounds and twenty-four races in 1990, and a first title for four-wheel drive
1990.note: Stuck won seven races in the Audi V8 quattro for Schmidt Motorsport Technik, giving the car its first championship. A rule change had outlawed turbocharged engines in favour of naturally aspirated ones, and the Audi suited the new formula better than the BMWs and Mercedes it beat.

1989.season: the 1989 season, the last of the first turbo era
1989.note: Ravaglia won three races in the BMW M3 Evo to take the title, and he was the first Italian champion in the series. It was the last year under heavily modified Group A rules with air restrictors, and the last DTM season to feature turbocharged engines until 2019.

1988.season: a first title in 1988, in a Ford
1988.note: Ludwig won the championship in the Ford Sierra RS500 Cosworth for Team Hein Gericke Ford Grab Motorsport, the first of three DTM titles he would take with three different manufacturers across seven years.

1987.season: the fourth season, in 1987, run to modified Group A rules
1987.note: Van de Poele won the championship in a BMW M3, the car that would define the late Group A years of the series. He was the first Belgian champion the DTM had.

1986.season: the 1986 season, the first to carry the Deutsche Tourenwagen Meisterschaft name
1986.note: Thiim won the title in a Rover Vitesse for ATN Autotechnik Nickel on 130 points, with victories at Zolder, Wunstorf and the Nürburgring, in his first year in the series after six seasons in single-seaters. He was the first Danish champion, and though he never won a second title he stayed near the front for a decade, finishing runner-up in 1992 and collecting nineteen wins in all.

1985.season: the 1985 season, the first with turbocharged cars
1985.note: Stureson won the championship in the Volvo 240 Turbo, the car everyone called the flying brick, taking two wins, three poles and two fastest laps. The series had gone international and admitted turbo engines that year, with handicap rules meant to hold them back against the naturally aspirated field. He was the first champion from outside Germany and the first of the turbo era.

1984.season: the first season, in 1984, won without a single race victory
1984.note: Strycek took the inaugural championship in a BMW 635 CSi without winning any of the fifteen races, which the scoring system of the time allowed. The series was called the Deutsche Produktionswagen Meisterschaft that first year and ran to modified Group A rules, with a grid that mixed the BMW with Rover Vitesses, Alfa Romeo GTV6s, Ford Capris, a Chevrolet Camaro and the Volvo 240 Turbo that would win the title the following season.
